I have sat as an arbitrator in more than sixty cases, and what surprises young lawyers is how early I make up my mind. Not about the case, about the argument. Within the first ten minutes I know whether counsel understands where the burden of proof lies. If it is on them, and they spend twenty minutes attacking a straw man, a version of the other side's case that nobody has actually made, I start to worry for them. What I want is the opposite. Tell me the strongest thing the other side will say, and then tell me why it is still wrong. It was that habit, more than any brilliant phrase, that won the best cases I have ever heard. And please, no red herrings. I can see when a point has been added only to distract me, and every point that does not move the case forward makes me trust the others a little less. Short, substantiated, and honest about its weaknesses: that is an argument that stands up to scrutiny.

I coach university debate teams, and the first exercise I give every new student is an uncomfortable one. They write their best argument, then they swap papers and spend fifteen minutes trying to poke holes in somebody else's. Not only does it teach them to attack, it shows them where their own argument is weak. What they discover is almost always the same. Some of them had cherry-picked their evidence: three studies that agreed with them, and none of the ten that did not. Others had built everything on a premise that nobody had checked. And many had used a slippery slope. If we allow this, then that will happen, and then disaster. It sounds powerful until somebody asks, why would the second step follow from the first? My students must have heard me say this a thousand times. If you can't find the weakness in your own line of reasoning, your opponent will, and he will find it in front of the judge.
